Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Greenville-Spartanburg SC
644 PM EST Tue Nov 24 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Confidence remains high for a storm system to impact the region 
Wednesday into Thursday with the potential for locally heavy rain 
and gusty winds. Rainfall amounts have decreased slightly, but a 
Wind Advisory has been issued for higher elevations of the mountains.

Updated the aviation discussion for the 00z TAFs.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1. A significant storm system is likely to impact the area
Wednesday into Thursday, Thanksgiving Day. There is potential
for frequent wind gusts strong enough to bring down temporary
outdoor structures such as tents and holiday decorations, and
perhaps isolated power outages. Widespread rainfall is expected,
with locally heavy rain possible but the flood risk currently
appearing low.
2. Gusty winds redevelop late Thursday and continue through Friday,
and light wintry precip becomes possible near the Tennessee
border. Warmer for the weekend.

.DISCUSSION...
Key message 1: A significant storm system is likely to impact the
area Wednesday into Thursday, Thanksgiving Day. There is potential
for frequent wind gusts strong enough to bring down temporary
outdoor structures such as tents and holiday decorations, and
perhaps isolated power outages. Widespread rainfall is expected,
with locally heavy rain possible but the flood risk currently
appearing low.

Sprawling surface high pressure, centered in the upper Mississippi
Valley as of Tuesday afternoon, is already beginning to build
southward along the Eastern Seaboard, driving gusty northeast
winds and a rapid decline in surface dewpoints since Tuesday
morning. This high will migrate eastward as a phased pair of
shortwaves moves across the Plains. By Wednesday morning the high
is expected to strengthen to 1040 mb or more under the confluent
upper flow downstream of the trough(s), resulting in classical
CAD that will be a major player in impacts along the East Coast,
and into our CWA, through at least Thursday morning.

A key difference among guidance members remains the disposition of
the southern shortwave, which looks to skirt along the Gulf Coast
tonight and Wednesday and induce cyclogenesis along a stalled front,
on the periphery of the damming high. Initially that shortwave will
induce pressure falls (if not actual cyclogenesis) near the Florida
Panhandle, helping to tighten the surface gradient tonight as the
wedge takes shape and drive development of a stout low-level jet
(LLJ) over the wedge. Wind gusts look to be maintained across the
area tonight and may even pick up overnight in the western CWA where
the wedge has the least influence and mixing should be a bit deeper.

Cloud cover increases from south to north tonight, but on account
of the already very low dewpoints in most of our area and strong
surface CAA, temps should fall into the mid to upper 30s over
most of the Piedmont tonight. A few locations near I-40, and in
mountain valleys nearer the Blue Ridge Escarpment, could fall below
freezing. Precip chances also increase from south to north over the
course of Wednesday. The most likely scenario still is that precip
doesn't begin until temperatures rise above freezing, and/or that
cloud cover keeps temps above freezing altogether. However, a recent
development is that some tiny QPF is spit out by the RRFS/REFS/HRRR
Wednesday morning where surface temps still are cold enough for
wintry precip. Per vertical profiles this probably would amount
only to a trace of sleet or snow, perhaps freezing rain if the
warm nose proves a little stronger than expected. It only takes a
trace of freezing rain or drizzle to cause travel difficulties,
and Wednesday will be a big travel day of course. However, with
temperatures being so close to freezing and the ground being warm,
only bridges or overpasses would be prone to become slippery,
if any wintry precip does result. We will monitor conditions
through this evening but the threat appears low and sparse enough
a Special Weather Statement is probably more justifiable than a
Winter Weather Advisory. Temperatures remain steady or even warm
Wednesday night as wedge erosion begins, and no wintry precip
appears possible then or Thursday morning.

Consensus is strengthening for a closed surface low to develop along
the east coast of Florida late Wednesday and track northward. ECMWF
appears to have maintained its more coastal track, and the GFS
the more inland track closer to Raleigh, so not much shift in
that sense; the GDPS may have trended slightly more toward the
GFS whereas it had been closer to the ECMWF. Moist easterly flow
over the damming high results in widespread precip for the CWA by
Wednesday evening, continuing overnight before generally tapering
off from SW to NE during the day on Thanksgiving. Ensemble QPF
thresholds remain pretty similar to earlier runs, if not having
trended slightly downward. Reflecting these trends, official
forecast QPF overall has trended downward this cycle. There
still is likely to be upslope enhancement where the easterly flow
intercepts the Blue Ridge Escarpment, and we maintain a 1-2" storm
total forecast in those areas, but many Piedmont locations now look
most likely to get an inch or less. However, REFS probs of even
1"/3hr are very low; 6hr ensemble max is only around 2" along the
eastern Escarpment. Very few global model ensemble members develop
QPF that is concerning for a flood risk. It does remain possible
a narrow frontogenetically forced band of heavy rain may develop
west of the low track, which models may not resolve well, so that
will continue to be evaluated as the worst-case scenario. In summary
the flash flood threat still looks low and perhaps secondary to the
threat posed by strong/gusty winds. WPC maintains a Marginal Risk
for most of our area on the Day 2 Excessive Rainfall Outlook, not
having upgraded any of our area to Slight on the latest issuance,
reflecting the lower QPF.

So, about the winds: As noted on previous forecast cycles this
event features anomalously strong easterly 925-850mb winds
associated with the LLJ, with winds of 45-50 kt possibly only a
couple thousand feet above ground over the Piedmont. Given the
strength of this wedge and the associated inversion, we continue
to expect only shallow mixing and thus gusts probably will be
limited in magnitude over the Piedmont. That said, in that area
there is good support among models for frequent 30-35 mph gusts
from Wednesday afternoon through Thursday morning, which seems
sensible after evaluating momentum transfer within the boundary
layer on REFS soundings. Peak winds for the event probably will be
closer to 40 mph. In warm advection regimes a strong LLJ does not
often translate to much gust potential for the mountains as gusts
cannot mix down easily, except the higher peaks which are closer to
being directly exposed to the jet, where gusts of 50 mph, perhaps
even higher, could result. Advisory level winds/gusts look likely
enough on ridgetops of the mountains that we have issued a Wind
Advisory for Avery County, and elevations above 3500 ft in Buncombe,
northern Jackson, and in counties bordering TN. Valid time Noon
Wed to 10 AM Thu. A few power outages very well could result in
those areas. If confidence increases on strong winds the Advisory
could be extended to lower elevations or other zones. Even where
no Advisory is in effect, the gusts certainly will be capable of
blowing over holiday decorations, tents, portable canopies, etc,
many of which are only rated for 25 mph gusts. One thing we might
not normally message: be prepared for wind to turn over outdoor
cooking appliances; have a fire extinguisher handy.

A noticeable lull in winds appears possible Thursday afternoon
as the system pulls away to the north and before CAA on its back
side induces strong mixing. Temps will return within a few degrees
of normal Thursday afternoon, but trend colder again Thursday
night. Light northwest-flow precip Thursday night may change to
a wintry mix if not snow or rime ice, and sufficient moisture
is seen in guidance to maintain a slight-chance PoP along the
TN border through Friday night. Accumulations are possible but
currently look to be light.

Temperatures trend warmer over the weekend; some guidance still
shows precip developing with a fast-moving shortwave circa Sunday
but the wetter scenarios are also on the warmer side, so for the
resultant small PoPs, only rain is mentioned.


Key message 2: Gusty winds redevelop late Thursday and continue
through Friday, and light wintry precip becomes possible near the
Tennessee border. Warmer for the weekend.

A noticeable lull in winds appears possible Thursday afternoon as
the system pulls away to the north and before CAA on its back side
induces strong mixing. Gusts are expected to return Thursday night
and continue through Friday. Can't completely rule out Advisory
level gusts in high mountain elevations, but the threat appears
lower compared to the Wed night and Thu event. Temps will return
within a few degrees of normal Thursday afternoon, but trend colder
again Thursday night. Light northwest-flow precip Thursday night
may change to a wintry mix if not snow or rime ice, and sufficient
moisture is seen in guidance to maintain a slight-chance PoP along
the TN border through Friday night. Accumulations are possible
but currently look to be light.

Temperatures trend warmer over the weekend; some guidance still
shows precip developing with a fast-moving shortwave circa Sunday
but the wetter scenarios are also on the warmer side, so for the
resultant small PoPs, only rain is mentioned.

.AVIATION /00Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
At KCLT and elsewhere: VFR expected thru daybreak, with increasing
mid clouds from south to north and cigs lowering to low-VFR
overnight. Winds will be out of the NE and expected to become
gustier thru the pre-dawn hours, except for KAVL, which will see
lighter winds.  Winds should pick up significantly on Wednesday
with gusts into the 25-30kt range at most sites thru the day and
into the evening.

Ceilings are expected to become MVFR mid- to late-morning, then
lower gradually in the aftn. Confidence on the timing of IFR is
still low, as fairly strong cold-air damming and steadier rain not
working in until this evening may hold IFR cigs off until early
evening. Rainfall looks to be mainly spotty and light thru the
daylight hours, then increase more in the 20-24z time frame and
continue thru the end of the 00z TAF period.

Outlook: Widespread rain, gusty winds and associated restrictions
should peak Wednesday night, then start to improve during the
day Thursday as a strong low pressure system tracks across the
terminals. Drier and VFR conditions still expected to return
Thursday night into Friday, but gusty winds will linger thru Friday
evening. Quiet weather expected on Saturday.
